name: Aaron Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi, and thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To begin, what's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights at Metro Fresh, the twenty-four-hour supermarket out by the industrial estate, ten to six. I start on the tills when the late crowd comes in, the shift workers and the taxi drivers, then from about two I'm restocking shelves and rotating dairy. Rosa, my partner, is a ward nurse, so we pass in the hallway like ships. I sleep in the afternoons while Leo and Mia are at school.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the quiet after two, when it's just the hum of the fridges and I can listen to a podcast with one earbud in. The wearing part is the body clock and the money. I'm forty-three and still on junior pay because I only moved from warehouse work to retail four years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say good, but I'd keep using the tools anyway, because they save me time. I'd tell my mates that hype cycles come and go. Online I'd mostly say nothing, but I might post something about how workers should get a share of whatever it saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, a plateau is fine for me in some ways, but it's not safe. Metro Fresh already put in four self-checkouts and a stock-count scanner, and I can see the night team shrinking by one every year. And we're one bill from trouble anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep using the chatbot, which I do every day to plan the stock rounds and write emails. I'd take an online course in inventory systems, because I'm curious and it might lead to a supervisor spot. I'd also put twenty pounds a week into a savings pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat. Not scared, but it's that low hum of money worry, like the fridges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the night team shrinking by one each year. How do you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I count. Two years ago there were six of us on nights, now there are four, and no one's replaced when they leave. Management says natural wastage, which is a fancy way of saying they don't have to sack anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you were the next one not replaced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd already have another thing lined up, like the inventory course or the supplier side. I'd look at the warehouse again, honestly, since I did that before. I'm the kind who has three plans, because I've been made redundant once.

say: I'd tell mates that **hype cycles** come and go, but I'd keep using the tools anyway.
I might post that workers should get a **share** of whatever AI saves.
think: Even a plateau isn't safe: Metro Fresh keeps adding **self-checkouts** and the night team shrinks yearly.
We're **one bill** from trouble in any world.
do: Keep using the **chatbot** daily to plan stock rounds and write emails.
Take an online course in **inventory systems** to aim for a supervisor spot.
Put **twenty pounds a week** into a savings pot.
feel: A bit **flat**, with a low hum of money worry like the fridges.
S0.quote: Two years ago there were six of us on nights, now there are four, and no one's replaced when they leave.
fieldNote: Aaron counts **headcount** himself, which gives him real evidence for his unease.
He already has a **backup plan** because he's been made redundant once.
His daily AI use makes the plateau feel like a **missed chance** as much as a relief.

steps.text: Use the chatbot daily to plan stock rounds
Take an online inventory systems course
Put twenty pounds a week into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the thinking jobs go first, but we're not far behind. I'd say we should be asking for training and a share of what the company saves. I'd post a thread about it, with the numbers on our team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm ahead of most people because I use this stuff daily. But the store will use software to decide who's needed, and nights are the easiest hours to cut. I might be the best prepared and still be the one let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the supervisor course and ask to help trial the new scanners and ordering tools, so I'm the person who knows them. I'd start learning basic Python in the evenings with the chatbot as a tutor. And I'd look into the maintenance side of the self-checkout machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit sick at the same time. There's a door opening, and the floor's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be best prepared but could still be let go. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because being good with tools isn't what the boss pays for on nights. The store pays for bodies on the floor, and when software says three people instead of four, being clever doesn't change the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a colleague who doesn't use AI at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show them in ten minutes how to ask it to write a message to the rota manager. Most of them are scared of it, not lazy. I'd rather share what I know than watch them get hurt.

say: I'd say the **thinking jobs** go first but we're not far behind.
I'd ask for **training** and a share of what the company saves.
think: I'm better prepared than most, but software could still cut my **night team** by one.
Being clever with tools doesn't change the **maths** when software says three people, not four.
do: Ask to **trial** the new scanners and ordering tools at the store.
Learn **basic Python** in the evenings with the chatbot as a tutor.
Look into the **maintenance** side of the self-checkout machines.
feel: **Excited** and a bit sick at once, with a door opening while the floor goes.
S1.quote: The store pays for bodies on the floor, and when software says three people instead of four, being clever doesn't change the maths.
fieldNote: Aaron's **adaptive** side shows in how he turns the threat into training plans.
He also knows readiness isn't enough, so his mood stays **anxious** rather than calm.
He offers to teach less confident colleagues, showing his **collective** instincts.

steps.text: Ask to trial new scanners and ordering tools
Learn basic Python in the evenings
Apply for self-checkout machine maintenance work
Show colleagues how to use the chatbot for messages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say get ready now, and I'd start a group chat with the night team for sharing what we know. Online I'd say the governments need a plan like yesterday, and that the people who profit should fund retraining. Two years isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, thinking AI comes in 2028 but the robots come in 2031. So I've got three years more than the office people. But the store will use the thinking side first to cut the schedules and orders, and probably the tills. Rosa's hospital ward is probably safer, and that's the thing keeping us afloat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on learning, evenings and days off, with the chatbot as my coach. I'd start in machine maintenance or robot servicing, as the robots arriving at stores need someone to fix them. I'd cut every extra bill and build one month, then two months, of savings. And I'd talk to Rosa so we agree on what happens if my pay stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. It's like the bit just before the rollercoaster drops. I feel afraid, but I'd rather be moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Rosa's job might be safer. How does that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we have one steady wage and one that might not be. So I'd be the one to take the risk, like training full time for a bit, but only if Rosa's job stays. If that went too, I wouldn't dare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it came this fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies racing to sell it, and the politicians who take their money. I'd say not the technology, it's the people deciding to leave the rest of us holding the bill.

say: I'd start a group chat with the **night team** to share what we know.
I'd say governments need a **plan** and profits should fund retraining.
think: Thinking AI arrives in 2028 but robots in **2031**, which gives me three more years than office workers.
The store will still cut **schedules, orders and tills** first.
do: Go all in on **learning** in evenings and days off, with the chatbot as coach.
Start training in **robot servicing**, since stores will need people to fix them.
Cut extra bills and build a **month, then two months**, of savings.
feel: **Wired**, like the moment before a rollercoaster drops, but moving beats waiting.
S2.quote: Thinking AI comes in 2028 but the robots come in 2031. So I've got three years more than the office people.
fieldNote: Aaron reads the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots as his window.
His plan depends on **Rosa's** nursing wage staying, so he'd take risks only while it does.
He blames **companies and politicians**, not the technology.

steps.text: Start a robot servicing course in the evenings
Build one then two months of savings
Start a night-team group chat to share information
Use the chatbot as a coach for new skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say there's time, so let's get organised, and I'd propose a union training fund. Online I'd write about what a fair share looks like, maybe a levy on the companies. I'd be the guy always sending links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years is long enough to switch tracks if I start right now. I'd be forty-eight, kids at eleven and fourteen, and I'd rather have a trade than a till. The scary bit is that everyone else will have the same idea at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd do an evening course, probably automation technician, and try to get day-release from Metro Fresh. I'd start a small side job fixing phones or setting up smart gadgets for neighbours with what I've learned. I'd keep saving the twenty a week, and bump it as the course ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a knot. I think I could win this one, but only if nothing else goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone else will have the same idea. What does that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The courses fill up and the jobs get competitive. So starting early matters, and being a bit better than other people matters. I'd rather be early and a bit wrong than late and right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Rosa's hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the course on hold and take extra shifts. The family comes first, always, but I'd go back to the course in the first gap. I've learned that when things go wrong you hold the line, then you get going again.

say: I'd say there's time, so let's get **organised**, and propose a union training fund.
I'd write about a **fair share** for workers, maybe a levy on the companies.
think: Five years is long enough to **switch tracks** if I start now, and I'd rather have a trade than a till.
Everyone will have the same idea at once, so **early** matters.
do: Do an evening course as an **automation technician** and ask for day-release.
Start a small **side job** setting up phones and smart gadgets for neighbours.
Keep saving **twenty a week** and raise it when the course ends.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a knot, because winning depends on nothing else going wrong.
S3.quote: I'd rather be early and a bit wrong than late and right.
fieldNote: Aaron's **plan** is specific: automation technician, day-release, side jobs.
He expects **crowded courses** and wants to move first.
His commitment to **family first** means he'd pause training if Rosa's hours changed.

steps.text: Do an evening automation technician course
Ask Metro Fresh for day-release to study
Fix phones and set up gadgets for neighbours
Keep saving twenty pounds a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say there's a decade, so look after yourselves and learn the stuff now. I'd push the union to make training a right. Online I'd share how to use these tools without fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, ten years is almost a relief. Leo would be nineteen and Mia sixteen, and I'd be fifty-three. I could change careers properly, even do a part-time degree, and have savings. But I'd still be a bit worried the whole thing happens faster than the date suggests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time diploma in automation or electronics within the first year, and aim to leave the tills in three or four. I'd turn the side job into something steadier, maybe fixing self-service kiosks for small shops. And I'd pay the mortgage down every time we got a bonus or tax rebate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Like a long runway. I'd still carry that money worry but it feels fixable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could knock the ten-year plan off course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money shocks, like a rise in rates, or Metro Fresh closing the night shift early. Or Rosa's hospital going to a robot-first model, which I'd not rule out. I'd keep a Plan B always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have by year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualification, three months of savings, and a customer or two for the side job. If I've got those, I'm not scared of 2039.

say: I'd say there's a decade, so **learn the tools** now and look after yourselves.
I'd push the union to make **training a right**.
think: Ten years is almost a **relief**, with the kids nineteen and sixteen and time to change careers.
I'd still worry the change comes **faster** than the date suggests.
do: Start a part-time **diploma** in automation or electronics in the first year.
Turn the side job into steady work fixing **self-service kiosks** for small shops.
Use any bonus or tax rebate to pay down the **mortgage**.
feel: **Pretty good**, like a long runway, with the money worry still fixable.
S4.quote: A qualification, three months of savings, and a customer or two for the side job. If I've got those, I'm not scared of 2039.
fieldNote: Aaron is **uneasy** rather than calm because money shocks could still derail things.
His five-year goals are **concrete**: a qualification, three months saved, a customer or two.
He keeps a **Plan B** because he's been made redundant before.

steps.text: Start a part-time automation or electronics diploma
Fix self-service kiosks for small shops
Put every bonus or rebate toward the mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's too fast to retrain properly and I've got no real cushion. What would help is a wage while I retrain, protection for my pension, and a say for workers in how the stores bring this in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd want it to happen. Honestly part of me wants it to happen, because it could make life easier for my kids if the gains are shared. What worries me is who gets to share.

headlineQuote: Honestly part of me wants it to happen, because it could make life easier for my kids if the gains are shared.
portrait: **Aaron** is 43, works nights on the tills and shelves at a twenty-four-hour supermarket, with a partner, two kids and a **mortgage**.
He has **under a month** saved and has watched his night team shrink from six to four.
He uses AI every day, takes risks, and turns each scenario into a **training plan**.
He blames **companies and politicians** for not sharing the gains, and would take risks only while his partner's nursing wage holds.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because it's too fast to retrain properly with no cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage while retraining**, pension protection, and a say for workers in how stores bring this in.
